rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown compounds across the window while encouraging all 10 to elute. This gives a first map of retention span, crowding, and whether stronger/weaker or steeper/shallower gradients are needed next.

Resolution is already perfect, so the only way to improve CRF is to shorten the analysis while keeping all 10 peaks observed and the closest cluster resolved. Halving the gradient is a safe first time-optimization step because the current minimum resolution margin is still comfortably high.

The 10 min gradient compressed the central cluster too much, with only one subcritical pair, so a small increase in gradient time should recover resolution while keeping the run very short. This targets the likely optimum between the well-resolved 20 min run and the over-compressed 10 min run.

The optimum appears near this region, and the limiting pair improves as tG increases, so the next logical step is a small further increase to try to push the last subcritical pair above threshold while preserving zero time penalty. This should test whether 14 min gives near-complete resolution without sacrificing too much speed.

At 14 min only one pair remains slightly below full resolution, and extending to 16 min should be enough to clear that pair while likely keeping the time penalty at zero. This is the most direct test for reaching the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The optimum in gradient time is clearly around 14 min, so now the best chance to gain the last bit of resolution without crossing into time penalty is to change selectivity slightly. A modest temperature decrease may open the critical 6/7 pair enough to reach full resolution while keeping the run close to the current best.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity, so test the opposite direction while keeping the best gradient time fixed. A small increase to 45 C may improve the critical mid-cluster separation enough to convert the 14 min method into a full-resolution, no-time-penalty optimum.

Temperature changes hurt, so keep T at 40 C and probe solvent-program selectivity instead. Lowering phi0 should reshape the early-to-mid gradient segment and may open the critical central pair without materially lengthening the run or losing any compounds.

Lowering phi0 was slightly worse than the current best, so test the opposite direction to see whether a slightly stronger start decompresses the critical mid-cluster more favorably. This is a focused selectivity probe around the near-optimal 14 min, 40 C condition.

Changing phi0 alone did not beat the current best, so now probe the other end of the gradient where the critical mid/late cluster is formed. A slightly lower phi1 may improve selectivity around the limiting pair while still eluting all compounds within the no-penalty time window.

Since the maximum CRF is already reached, use the remaining injections to map robustness around the optimum. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether full resolution is maintained with a slightly weaker final strength and potentially different selectivity near the critical pair.

With the optimum already found, a useful final local probe is whether a shorter gradient can preserve full resolution at the improved phi1. This tests if the phi1 shift to 0.85 also allows a faster method with CRF still at or near the maximum.

Now that phi1 = 0.85 gave full resolution at 40 C, test temperature robustness around the optimum rather than speed. A small increase to 45 C checks whether the improved phi1 setting preserves baseline separation under a warmer condition.

The optimum is sharp in temperature, so return to 40 C and test whether a slightly stronger starting composition keeps full resolution with the improved phi1. This is a local robustness check on phi0 around the proven optimum.

A second maximum at phi0 = 0.15 suggests the optimum may extend toward a slightly stronger start. Testing phi0 = 0.20 maps that plateau and may identify an equally optimal but more aggressive, robust operating point.

Two exact-optimum points at phi0 = 0.10 and 0.15 suggest a narrow but real plateau, so testing phi0 = 0.05 defines the lower edge at the same phi1. This maps robustness around the optimum while staying close to conditions already proven to elute all compounds cleanly.

The best-performing region is now clearly centered at phi1 = 0.85 and phi0 = 0.10–0.15, so test whether the stronger-start optimum at phi0 = 0.15 can support a shorter 12 min gradient. This checks for a faster local optimum while remaining very close to a proven CRF 1.000 method.

A 12 min gradient at the second optimum lost critical-pair resolution, so the useful remaining check is the upper side of the local optimum in gradient time. This confirms the robustness window around the CRF 1.000 condition and whether extra resolution is gained at the cost of time, as seen for the phi0 = 0.10 series.

With two exact optima already secured, the most informative remaining experiments are boundary checks in the local neighborhood. Testing phi0 = 0.20 at phi1 = 0.90 distinguishes whether the poorer result at phi0 = 0.20 came mainly from the stronger start itself or from interaction with the lower phi1 setting.

You already have CRF 1.000, so the remaining value is defining the optimal neighborhood. Testing phi0 = 0.15 with a lower phi1 checks whether the second optimum at phi0 = 0.15 remains fully resolved when the gradient end strength is reduced, complementing the phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.80 result.

With the score ceiling already reached, the best use of remaining runs is robustness mapping around the optimum. Testing the proven phi1 = 0.85 optimum at 35 C complements the failed 45 C experiment and shows whether cooler operation preserves full resolution at this improved selectivity setting.

The optimum is clearly temperature-sensitive, but it is still useful to test whether the phi0 = 0.15 optimum is more tolerant to cooling than the phi0 = 0.10 optimum. This is a focused robustness comparison between the two CRF 1.000 methods.

The remaining informative check is the warm-side robustness of the second CRF 1.000 optimum. This completes the local temperature map for the best phi0/phi1 combination and confirms whether the selectivity collapse at higher temperature is general.

With the optimum already secured, the last two runs can finish mapping the stronger-start/lower-end-strength corner near the best region. This tests whether the loss at phi0 = 0.20 is intrinsic even when paired with the slower-eluting phi1 = 0.80 setting that maintained full resolution at phi0 = 0.15.

A third CRF 1.000 point at phi0 = 0.20, phi1 = 0.80 suggests the optimum ridge extends toward stronger starts when phi1 is reduced. The final run should test the next grid point to define the upper boundary of that ridge and see whether full resolution is still maintained.
